lessons.title: Differentiate masked focal loss under class imbalance
lessons.body:
# Differentiate masked focal loss under class imbalance

Focal weighting changes which examples dominate the gradient. The factor depends on the current model probability and must participate in autograd; multiplying cross entropy by a detached difficulty score defines a different update. A declared reduction also matters when class weights and ignored examples interact. This Lab uses multiclass logits, one integer target per row and a fixed valid-row denominator. It exercises extreme scores and an entirely ignored batch without introducing undefined gradients.

## Prepare offline

Choose Download entire course or Download entire category first. After completion, code and checks run locally on CPU. The independent example needs no account, remote service or API key.

```python
import torch
x = torch.tensor([[2., 0.]])
print(x.log_softmax(-1).exp())
```

## Review the evidence

Compare gamma zero with cross entropy, then inspect derivatives at a difficult example. Explain why class weighting, focal weighting and resampling are different interventions. Measure rare-group errors on held-out data before choosing them.
lessons.task: Implement multiclass focal loss: mean of -alpha[y]*(1-p[y])**gamma*log(p[y]) over valid rows, normalized by the number of valid targets, not the sum of class weights. Use log-softmax, preserve autograd and return graph-connected zero when every target is ignored. Reject nonfinite logits, invalid shapes/dtypes/labels, negative or nonfinite gamma, and nonpositive/nonfinite class weights. Do not detach the focal factor.

lessons.title: Own both passes of a sharpness-aware optimizer step
lessons.body:
# Own both passes of a sharpness-aware optimizer step

Sharpness-aware training evaluates a nearby parameter vector before making the real update. Two forward passes are not two optimizer steps. The second gradient belongs to the perturbed model, while momentum and weight decay must update the original model exactly once. Reversing a floating-point perturbation by subtraction can leave rounding residue, so this exercise owns exact snapshots. Exception handling is part of the algorithm: a failed closure must never leave the live model perturbed.

## Prepare offline

Choose Download entire course or Download entire category first. After completion, code and checks run locally on CPU. The independent example needs no account, remote service or API key.

```python
import torch
w = torch.tensor([3., 4.])
print(w / w.norm())
```

## Review the evidence

Explain which gradient is used and when optimizer state advances. A stochastic or stateful model additionally needs an explicit policy for randomness and running buffers; passing this deterministic fixture does not resolve that policy.

Compute the global first-pass norm, perturb trainable parameters in that direction by rho, recompute gradients, restore exact original parameter values and apply exactly one optimizer step using second-pass gradients. Always restore parameters and clear gradients if the second pass fails. Reject invalid rho, nonfinite losses/gradients, duplicate or incomplete optimizer ownership. This fixture uses deterministic layers without BatchNorm or dropout; stateful stochastic layers need a separate replay/buffer policy.

lessons.title: Project conflicting task gradients without mutating their owners
lessons.body:
# Project conflicting task gradients without mutating their owners

Multi-task objectives can produce gradients that oppose one another even when the shared model is differentiable. PCGrad edits a task gradient by removing conflicting components relative to original peer gradients. Projection order matters with three or more tasks, so order and randomness are part of the reproducibility contract. Returning separate rows preserves the distinction between surgery and the later task-weighting decision. This is a local vector algorithm; it does not claim a Pareto optimum or execute distributed reduction.

## Prepare offline

Choose Download entire course or Download entire category first. After completion, code and checks run locally on CPU. The independent example needs no account, remote service or API key.

```python
import torch
a = torch.tensor([1., -1.])
b = torch.tensor([0., 1.])
print(torch.dot(a, b))
```

## Review the evidence

Compare original and projected directions on several task geometries. Audit parameter alignment, missing gradients and aggregation weights before applying surgery to real shared and task-specific model parameters.
lessons.task: Return a detached [tasks, parameters] matrix of PCGrad gradients. For each task, visit the other ORIGINAL task gradients in a seed-local shuffled order. If the current projected gradient has a negative dot product with an original peer, remove that component. Skip zero-norm peers. Do not mutate the input or global RNG. The caller chooses how to combine the projected rows; this Lab does not assert that a mean improves every task.
lessons.starter:
import random
import torch

def project_conflicts(gradients, seed=0):
    # TODO: implement project_conflicts under the declared contract.
    return None
lessons.solution:
import random
import torch

def project_conflicts(gradients, seed=0):
    if gradients.ndim!=2 or gradients.shape[0]<2 or gradients.shape[1]==0 or not gradients.is_floating_point() or not torch.isfinite(gradients).all():
        raise ValueError('Expected finite floating [tasks>=2, parameters>0] gradients.')
    original=gradients.detach().clone()
    projected=original.clone()
    rng=random.Random(seed)
    for task in range(len(original)):
        order=[j for j in range(len(original)) if j!=task]
        rng.shuffle(order)
        for peer in order:
            norm=original[peer].square().sum()
            conflict=torch.dot(projected[task],original[peer])
            if norm>0 and conflict<0:
                projected[task]=projected[task]-conflict/norm*original[peer]
    return projected

lessons.title: Update a detached Group DRO adversary from group means
lessons.body:
# Update a detached Group DRO adversary from group means

Average risk can hide a poorly served subgroup when that group is rare. Group DRO maintains an adversary over declared groups, increasing mass on groups with larger observed mean loss. The adversary state is an optimization state, not a differentiable shortcut through every previous batch. Normalizing by each group count prevents duplicated rows from becoming an unintended group weight. Observing only a subset of groups requires an explicit estimator; this exercise instead declares complete group coverage per batch.

## Prepare offline

Choose Download entire course or Download entire category first. After completion, code and checks run locally on CPU. The independent example needs no account, remote service or API key.

```python
import torch
log_q = torch.tensor([0., 2.])
print(log_q.log_softmax(0).exp())
```

## Review the evidence

Separate group definition, adversary optimization and final evaluation. Compare average and worst-group held-out results with an ERM baseline; training group weights alone are not evidence of robustness under unseen shifts.
lessons.task: Return (robust_loss, next_log_weights). All G declared groups must occur in this batch. Average losses within each group, update adversary log weights by eta times DETACHED group means, normalize in log space, then weight differentiable group means by detached updated probabilities. Do not backpropagate into old adversary state. Reject empty/missing/out-of-range groups, nonfinite losses/state and nonpositive eta. This deliberately balanced-batch contract avoids silently inventing loss for unobserved groups.

lessons.title: Fit a positive heteroscedastic Gaussian likelihood
lessons.body:
# Fit a positive heteroscedastic Gaussian likelihood

A regression model can learn both a conditional mean and input-dependent noise. Gaussian likelihood rewards a good mean but also penalizes excessive variance, unlike simply enlarging every interval. An unconstrained raw output is transformed into a positive variance before any logarithm or division. Very negative raw values test the numerical behavior at the floor. The learned quantity is aleatoric uncertainty under this likelihood assumption; it does not include model uncertainty or automatically provide calibrated prediction intervals.

## Prepare offline

Choose Download entire course or Download entire category first. After completion, code and checks run locally on CPU. The independent example needs no account, remote service or API key.

```python
import torch
from torch.nn import functional as F
raw = torch.tensor([-50., 0., 3.])
print(F.softplus(raw) + 1e-4)
```

## Review the evidence

Keep variance distinct from standard deviation. Evaluate log loss and interval coverage on held-out data, and inspect results by region; a good average likelihood can coexist with subgroup miscalibration.
lessons.task: Use variance=softplus(raw_variance)+floor and return mean(0.5*(log(2*pi)+log(variance)+(target-mean)**2/variance)). Preserve gradients through both mean and raw variance. Require aligned nonempty finite floating tensors and finite floor>0. The floor is part of the declared model; do not clamp a negative variance after taking its logarithm.

lessons.title: Train through per-channel fake quantization and saturation
lessons.body:
# Train through per-channel fake quantization and saturation

Quantization-aware training simulates rounding during training so the model can adapt to a finite grid. Rounding has almost-everywhere zero derivative; a declared straight-through rule supplies the training surrogate. Saturation still needs a policy: this exercise passes gradients inside the representable interval and stops them outside it. Per-channel scales prevent one large output row from determining every row’s resolution. The result remains floating point and is not evidence of compressed storage, integer execution or faster inference.

## Prepare offline

Choose Download entire course or Download entire category first. After completion, code and checks run locally on CPU. The independent example needs no account, remote service or API key.

```python
import torch
x = torch.tensor([.5, 1.5, 2.5])
print(x.round())
```

## Review the evidence

Inspect clipping rates, the scale calibration set and post-conversion error separately. Compare a floating baseline with a real deployed quantized runtime before claiming memory or latency savings.

Round ties to even, simulate quantize/dequantize in floating point and use straight-through rounding with zero gradient outside the clipping interval. Return a floating tensor; this is QAT simulation, not a packed int8 kernel or a speed benchmark.

lessons.title: Project: audit ERM and Group DRO under a spurious correlation
lessons.body:
# Project: audit ERM and Group DRO under a spurious correlation

A majority-aligned shortcut can make average accuracy look reassuring while minority groups fail. This experiment creates that failure mode explicitly with generated causal and spurious features, then compares two actual optimizer objectives from the same initialization. Validation selects checkpoints before test labels are observed. Reports retain per-group results, row identities and a reloadable artifact rather than declaring that a robust objective must win every seed. The data are a controlled synthetic stress test, not real-world robustness evidence.

## Prepare offline

Choose Download entire course or Download entire category first. After completion, code and checks run locally on CPU. The independent example needs no account, remote service or API key.

```python
import torch
labels = torch.tensor([0, 0, 1, 1])
shortcut = torch.tensor([0, 1, 0, 1])
print((labels == shortcut).float().mean())
```

## Review the evidence

Run several seeds and compare validation selection, average test accuracy and the worst group. Explain how group definition, regularization and a shift outside the declared groups can change the conclusion.
lessons.task: Implement the complete experiment using the supplied make_data/tensors/classification/train_model helpers. Generate the declared local synthetic four-group dataset, train ERM and Group DRO from identical initialization, choose each checkpoint only by validation worst-group accuracy then validation loss, and evaluate the untouched test set once. Return the reference schema with both models, disjoint row IDs, train/validation fit hash, source hash, measured history and a real serialized artifact. The artifact includes both model states and initialization for independent audit. Reload into a fresh model and verify predictions. Test-label overrides must affect only evaluation, never selection or weights. The reference CLI writes model/report files in the current project. Report empirical sample group masses for ERM and the adversary probabilities belonging to the selected DRO checkpoint; serialize those probabilities and selected step with each model.

lessons.title: Project: train uncertainty and calibrate independent prediction intervals
lessons.body:
# Project: train uncertainty and calibrate independent prediction intervals

An uncertainty model and an interval calibration procedure answer different questions. This project trains a heteroscedastic likelihood, selects its checkpoint on validation data, and only then uses a separate calibration partition to choose interval width. The corrected order statistic is an integer rank, not an interpolated percentile. Final test rows measure observed coverage without feeding back into model or quantile selection. Synthetic regions make subgroup differences visible while keeping every row reproducible offline.

## Prepare offline

Choose Download entire course or Download entire category first. After completion, code and checks run locally on CPU. The independent example needs no account, remote service or API key.

```python
import math
n = 128
alpha = .1
print(math.ceil((n+1)*(1-alpha)))
```

## Review the evidence

Explain the exchangeability assumption and the distinction between marginal, conditional and subgroup coverage. Refit on shifted data only with a new evaluation protocol; a single observed coverage number is not a universal guarantee.
lessons.task: Build the complete local synthetic heteroscedastic regression experiment with four disjoint partitions: training, validation selection, conformal calibration and final test. Train both mean and positive variance using Gaussian NLL, choose the checkpoint by validation NLL, then compute normalized absolute calibration residuals and the finite-sample ceil((n+1)*(1-alpha)) order statistic without interpolation. Export the learned state plus quantile, reload in a fresh model, and report actual test coverage, width and left/right-region coverage. Calibration and test labels must never fit or select model weights. Keep the full reference report schema. Marginal conformal coverage requires exchangeability and does not imply subgroup coverage.

checks.name: actual likelihood training and calibrated held-out evidence
checks.code:
r = run_experiment(7, 70)
assert r['train_nll'] < r['initial_train_nll'] and 0 <= r['test']['coverage'] <= 1 and (r['test']['mean_width'] > 0) and (len(r['test']['group_coverage']) == 2), 'Contract failed: actual likelihood training and calibrated held-out evidence.'
assert 1 <= r['best_step'] <= 70 and len(r['history']) >= 4, 'Contract failed: actual likelihood training and calibrated held-out evidence.'

checks.name: quantile equals the independent corrected calibration rank
checks.code:
r = run_experiment(8, 35)
saved = read_payload(r['artifact'])
m = build_model()
m.load_state_dict(saved['state'])
rows = make_data(8)['calibration']
mean, std = predictions(m, rows)
_, y = tensors(rows)
values = sorted(((y - mean).abs() / std).tolist())
rank = math.ceil((len(values) + 1) * 0.9)
assert r['rank'] == rank and abs(r['q'] - values[rank - 1]) < 1e-06, 'Contract failed: quantile equals the independent corrected calibration rank.'

checks.name: test and calibration labels never fit the model
checks.code:
data = make_data(9)
test = copy.deepcopy(data['test'])
cal = copy.deepcopy(data['calibration'])
for row in test:
    row['y'] += 30
for row in cal:
    row['y'] += 10
a = run_experiment(9, 30)
b = run_experiment(9, 30, 0.1, test, cal)
pa = read_payload(a['artifact'])
pb = read_payload(b['artifact'])
assert a['fit_hash'] == b['fit_hash'] and all((torch.equal(v, pb['state'][k]) for k, v in pa['state'].items())) and (b['q'] > a['q']), 'Contract failed: test and calibration labels never fit the model.'

a = read_payload(r['artifact'])
m = build_model()
m.load_state_dict(a['state'])
assert interval_metrics(m, make_data(3)['test'], a['q']) == r['test'] and r['reload_max_error'] == 0 and (r['artifact_bytes'] > 1000), 'Contract failed: fresh reload and all four partitions preserve ownership.'

assert len(sets) == 4 and all((not left & right for i, left in enumerate(sets) for right in sets[i + 1:])), 'Contract failed: fresh reload and all four partitions preserve ownership.'
